{"artifact":"SmeDossierEnvelope","schema_version":"0.4.0","stage_id":"02.dossier_sections","probe":"rdmv-sc-d","lineage":{"input_manifest_sha256":"91ae45efd95e43e9de58d899c582d54ec8d7ca2f2e3e333b7bfb1b74dbef8efa","candidate_lineage_id":"2026-10-28-rdmv-sc-class-d:lineage:88","source_registry_sha256":"61c32f86a25e3c021742b3c9ddf64a97709817dd75a19df6d2b69eac0a40c4f1","source_liveness_sha256":"feb7871590284d2a19ab0509ff65b48154ba15e637a6ec9b839f55a72736ffdb"},"envelope_scope":{"kind":"partial_chunk","assigned_section_ids":["C"],"chunk_index":1,"chunk_total":1},"section_char_limit":12000,"sections":[{"section_id":"C","chunk_id":"C.01","merge_seq":1,"domain":"General driving: turns, turnabouts, intersections, special interchanges, roundabouts and school bus stops","heading":"C — Turning rules, two-point and three-point turnabouts, intersection searching, diverging diamond and RCUT designs, roundabouts and when to stop for a school bus","learner_facing":true,"markdown":"## C — Turning rules, two-point and three-point turnabouts, intersection searching, diverging diamond and RCUT designs, roundabouts and when to stop for a school bus
Knowledge domain: how a South Carolina driver turns and reverses direction safely, what to search for and when to move at intersections, how diverging diamond interchanges, restricted crossing U-turn intersections and roundabouts work, and when the law requires stopping for a school bus.

FACT_ID: sec09-F01 | anchor: A01
Before turning, search every corner for traffic controls, pedestrians and other vehicles, and signal what you intend to do. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec09-F02 | anchor: A01
Get into and stay in the lane nearest the direction you plan to turn. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec09-F03 | anchor: A01
During a turn, look through it to the farthest point you can see along your intended path. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec09-F04 | anchor: A01
On a right turn, avoid swinging wide to the left before you turn. [A01]
Source: [A01 -> pdf-0075]

FACT_ID: sec09-F05 | anchor: A02
Always make a right turn from the right-most part of your lane. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec09-F06 | anchor: A02
When turning left, yield to oncoming traffic and always turn from the left-most part of your lane. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec09-F07 | anchor: A02
A two-point turnabout uses a street, alley or driveway to reverse your direction when driving around a block is impractical or impossible. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec09-F08 | anchor: A02
For a reverse two-point turnabout, signal right, stop and check traffic to the sides and rear, then back up until your rear bumper reaches the near edge of the driveway. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec09-F09 | anchor: A02
While backing slowly into the driveway, steer quickly all the way to the right, then straighten the wheels and stop once the vehicle is centered in the driveway. [A02]
Source: [A02 -> pdf-0076]

FACT_ID: sec09-F10 | anchor: A03
For a forward two-point turnabout, check your mirrors, signal left, ease toward the road's center, then pull into the alley or driveway keeping as far to its left side as you can. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec09-F11 | anchor: A03
In the forward two-point turnabout, stop when the rear of the vehicle clears the curb or driveway edge, check every direction, signal right and shift into reverse. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec09-F12 | anchor: A03
Use a three-point turnabout only when the street is too narrow for a U-turn and you cannot go around the block, and only on a two-lane road that is not busy. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec09-F13 | anchor: A03
A three-point turn must be done without hitting the curb, leaving the road surface or using a side street or driveway. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec09-F14 | anchor: A03
Three-point step one: check the mirrors, turn on the right signal to show you are pulling to the right edge, and stop there. [A03]
Source: [A03 -> pdf-0077]

FACT_ID: sec09-F15 | anchor: A04
Three-point step two: signal left, check traffic and your left blind spot over your shoulder, then turn hard left across the road and stop when you reach the other side [A04] [A03].
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec09-F16 | anchor: A04
Three-point step three: shift to reverse, check traffic and both blind spots over your shoulders instead of trusting the rearview mirror alone, then turn hard right back across and stop. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec09-F17 | anchor: A04
Three-point step four: shift to drive, check traffic and blind spots, turn hard left into the right lane of the new direction, make sure the signal has cancelled and drive straight on. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec09-F18 | anchor: A04
Whenever you reach an intersection, reduce speed and scan for traffic controls, cross and oncoming traffic, people walking or cycling, the state of the road and spots where you cannot see well. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec09-F19 | anchor: A04
Do not depend on other road users to obey signals or signs, because you can control only your own driving. [A04]
Source: [A04 -> pdf-0078]

FACT_ID: sec09-F20 | anchor: A05
Some road users may not yield the right-of-way, so always be prepared to avoid a collision. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec09-F21 | anchor: A05
Once you have stopped at an intersection, give yourself extra time to spot crossing vehicles and bicyclists, and look left, then right, then left again before you enter. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec09-F22 | anchor: A05
When a light turns green, do not move straight into the intersection; first make sure your path is clear and no traffic is crossing. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec09-F23 | anchor: A05
Do not turn into a lane just because an approaching vehicle is signaling, since the driver may plan to turn after passing you or may have left the signal on from an earlier turn. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec09-F24 | anchor: A05
A diverging diamond interchange, or DDI, differs from a conventional interchange in its directional crossovers on either side, which spare left-turning vehicles from crossing the path of oncoming through traffic. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec09-F25 | anchor: A05
The DDI design has improved turning movements to and from the interstate and sharply cut vehicle-to-vehicle conflict points compared with a conventional diamond interchange. [A05]
Source: [A05 -> pdf-0079]

FACT_ID: sec09-F26 | anchor: A06
A restricted crossing U-turn, or RCUT, intersection removes left-turn and through movements from the cross street approaches. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec09-F27 | anchor: A06
At an RCUT, drivers coming from the cross street turn right onto the main road and then make a U-turn at a one-way median opening. [A06]
Source: [A06 -> pdf-0080]

FACT_ID: sec09-F28 | anchor: A07
A roundabout, also known as a traffic circle, is a circular intersection where vehicles travel counterclockwise around a raised center island and entering traffic yields to circulating traffic. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec09-F29 | anchor: A07
Slow down as you enter a roundabout or traffic circle, which a warning sign may announce ahead of time. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec09-F30 | anchor: A07
Yield to the traffic already in the roundabout, enter in a counterclockwise direction, then go to your exit, signal and leave. [A07]
Source: [A07 -> pdf-0081]

FACT_ID: sec09-F31 | anchor: A08
Roundabouts are safer than traditional intersections because they remove head-on and high-speed right-angle collisions. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec09-F32 | anchor: A08
For as long as a school bus is stopped or getting ready to stop with red or amber lights flashing or its stop arm out, you must remain stopped. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec09-F33 | anchor: A08
After the school bus lights stop flashing and the stop arm can no longer be seen, move on slowly and watch for children. [A08]
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec09-F34 | anchor: A08
On a two-lane road you are required to stop for a stopped school bus, whether you are meeting it or following it [A08] [A09].
Source: [A08 -> pdf-0082]

FACT_ID: sec09-F35 | anchor: A09
On a four-lane or other multi-lane highway, the school bus stopping rule applies only when you are traveling behind the bus. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec09-F36 | anchor: A09
You must also stop when you are trying to pass a school bus whose red or amber signals are flashing. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0083]

FACT_ID: sec09-F37 | anchor: A09
You need not stop when the school bus sits in a passenger loading zone entirely off the main travel lanes and pedestrians are not permitted to cross the road. [A09]
Source: [A09 -> pdf-0083]

Misconceptions: a green light does not mean go at once, because crossing traffic may still be clearing; another driver's turn signal does not prove they will turn; a three-point turn may not use a driveway, while a two-point turnabout does; amber flashing lights on a stopping school bus already require you to stop; on a multi-lane highway the stopping rule covers drivers behind the bus, while on a two-lane road it covers drivers in both directions.
Mnemonics: right turns hug the right, left turns hug the left; at a stop, look left, right, left; roundabouts go counterclockwise and entering traffic gives way; two-lane road, everyone stops for the bus.
Glossary: turnabout means a maneuver that reverses your direction of travel; DDI means diverging diamond interchange; RCUT means restricted crossing U-turn intersection; roundabout means a circular intersection around a raised center island, also called a traffic circle; stop arm means the sign arm a school bus extends when it stops.
